Both are silent — the ids are generated in several places (charterExtractionLane, conceptualPerspectiveLane, GATE_LANES), so uniqueness currently rests on caller discipline rather than on the chokepoint that claims it. A throw on a repeated id or promptFilename within one call would make the stated invariant mechanical.

finding.title: parseUnifiedDiffHunks misreads an added line beginning with '++' as a new file header
finding.summary: The parser classifies any diff line starting with `+++ ` as a file header. An ADDED content line whose text begins with `++ ` is rendered as `+++ …` in a unified diff, so the parser silently re-points currentFile at a bogus path and attributes every following hunk to it — the hunk map is wrong with `available: true`, defeating the fail-closed intent that same-file overlaps are never silently dropped.
evidence: common.ts:222 `if (rawLine.startsWith("+++ ")) {` — the check is unconditional on diff position; there is no state distinguishing a header region from a hunk body.
common.ts:230-231 the remainder is taken as the path (`b/` stripped) and assigned to currentFile.
common.ts:246 subsequent `@@` hunks are pushed with that mis-derived `currentFile`.

Contrast with the module's own stated contract at common.ts:170-176: on anything it cannot parse the result must be unavailable so callers fail closed; this path instead returns available:true with wrong data.

reproduction: A branch adds a line whose content is `++ note` (e.g. inside a markdown or embedded-diff fixture).
`git diff HEAD...branch` renders that line as `+++ note`.
parseUnifiedDiffHunks sets currentFile to `note`; all later hunks of that file are recorded under `note`, so an overlap check against the real path finds none.

finding.title: deriveAccessMemory takes the run id from whichever ledger entry happens to carry one first
finding.summary: src/audit/orchestrator/accessMemory.ts:38 resolves the record's run identity as `options.runId ?? results.find((r) => r.run_id)?.run_id`. The ledger is append-only across the audit and can legitimately contain results from more than one run (a resumed run, or a re-dispatch after a new run id was minted); nothing here checks that the ledger is single-run. When callers omit options.runId, the derived access-memory record is therefore stamped with the run id of the EARLIEST result carrying one, silently attributing the whole aggregated touch stream — including touches from later runs — to a stale run. Because the doc comment promises a per-run record whose bytes are a pure function of the ledger, this misattribution is invisible downstream. Either require runId, or refuse (or record all ids) when the ledger spans more than one.

entries.title: quoteForCmd quotes only whitespace/quote characters, so a cmd metacharacter in an argument is interpreted by cmd.exe
entries.rationale: Finding excluded by the intent checkpoint (filter or excluded scope).

finding.title: quoteForCmd quotes only whitespace/quote characters, so a cmd metacharacter in an argument is interpreted by cmd.exe
finding.summary: resolveSpawn re-renders the whole command line into a single `cmd /d /s /c "..."` string, but quoteForCmd only wraps an argument when it contains whitespace or a double quote (`if (!/[\s"]/u.test(arg)) return arg;`). An argument such as `a&b`, `x|y`, `a^b`, `%PATH%` or `>out` is therefore emitted BARE into a cmd command line, where `&`, `|`, `^`, `<`, `>` are command separators/redirections and `%…%` is variable expansion. On win32 this silently changes what runs — argument splitting, a swallowed redirection, or (with attacker- or path-derived text) command injection — while the same call on darwin/linux passes the argument through untouched, so the failure is platform-divergent and invisible to a POSIX CI leg.
evidence: scripts/shared/spawn-shell.mjs:10 `if (!/[\s"]/u.test(arg)) return arg;` — no cmd metacharacter class is considered.
scripts/shared/spawn-shell.mjs:21 `args: ["/d", "/s", "/c", [command, ...args].map(quoteForCmd).join(" ")]` — the joined string IS a cmd command line, so anything unquoted is parsed by cmd.
Consumers pass caller-supplied argv: smoke-process.mjs:73 `resolveSpawn(command, args)` and profile.mjs:54 `resolveSpawn(command, args)`.
runtime:unit:scripts-shared: not_confirmed — Deterministic runtime command failed with exit code 1: npm test
reproduction: On win32, call resolveSpawn("npm.cmd", ["run", "a&whoami"]) and inspect the produced args: the argument is emitted unquoted, so cmd treats `&whoami` as a second command.

finding.title: sameLensDedupe lacks crossLensDedupe's absorbed-survivor guard: an absorbed finding keeps absorbing, and its victims are dropped from the output
finding.summary: Deepening pass on SHARED-P3-COR-001: the finding STANDS at HEAD, unchanged at high/high. In sameLensDedupe the inner loop (lines 548-568) re-checks only `removed.has(group[j])`; it never re-checks `removed.has(group[i])` after the i-slot finding is itself absorbed on the `!keepA` branch (lines 564-567). The sibling crossLensDedupe carries exactly that guard at line 292 and documents it as a conservation requirement, not an optimization. Consequence at HEAD: once group[i] is absorbed, it stays a live survivor candidate for the remaining j; when it wins a later pair, the partner is added to `removed` and merged into an object the terminal filter at line 572 discards, so that partner's affected_files/evidence vanish from the report (data loss). The mirror case is duplication rather than loss: an already-removed group[i] that LOSES a later pair is absorbed a second time, so its evidence is unioned into two different survivors. Scope is exactly sameLensDedupe (the audit-side same-lens pass); crossLensDedupe and upsertFindingByIdentity are unaffected, so the finding should stand as written rather than widen. The missing guard is unconditional in the sibling ('not policy-gated; conservation'), so this is not a policy divergence between the two draws — it is a one-core drift in the audit draw.

finding.title: Persisted audit-scope file arrays are ordered with locale-sensitive localeCompare instead of code-unit order
finding.summary: computeAuditScope sorts seed_files and expanded_files with a.localeCompare(b) (scope.ts:166,169); those arrays are returned verbatim in the persisted AuditScopeManifest (scope.ts:184-185). localeCompare is ICU/locale-dependent and does not agree with code-unit ordering for paths containing punctuation, digits or mixed case (ICU treats '-' and '_' as variable-weight, so e.g. 'src/a-b.ts' vs 'src/ab.ts' and 'src/B.ts' vs 'src/a.ts' order differently than a '<' comparison). finding.title: Louvain local-moving never isolates a node: the zero-gain baseline is bound to the node's current community, not a singleton
finding.summary: localMoving (src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:246-274) initializes `bestGain = 0` with `bestCommunity = current`, and the comment states the baseline is 'staying in a fresh singleton'. finding.title: Captured child output can be truncated: run() resolves on 'exit', not 'close'
finding.summary: In audit-code-wrapper-lib.mjs, run() with { capture: true } pipes stdout/stderr and resolves the promise from the child's 'exit' event. finding.title: The Python import scanner has no triple-quoted-string state, so import lines inside docstrings become real graph edges
finding.summary: pythonLogicalLines (src/audit/extractors/graphPythonImports.ts:54-85) processes the file line-by-line and tracks only quote state WITHIN a line (scanStringAware with `"` and `'`) plus parenthesis depth and backslash continuations. Triple-quoted strings — the dominant form of Python docstrings, and the place where usage examples like `import numpy as np` or `from .core import Widget` most often appear — carry no multi-line state, so their contents are treated as ordinary source lines. finding.summary: On win32 the probe builds exactly one candidate name, `${command}.exe` (line 114), and walks PATH looking only for that. finding.title: Locale-dependent localeCompare orders derived ids and persisted arrays in the decompose layer
finding.summary: consensus.ts and charterExtraction.ts order content-derived arrays and pick ids with `String.prototype.localeCompare` called with no locale/collation argument — its result depends on the host's default ICU locale and ICU version, so ordering is not guaranteed identical across environments. This drives real identity, not just presentation: UnionFind.union picks the representative by localeCompare (consensus.ts:148), `node_id: members[0]` takes the first element of a localeCompare-sorted member list (consensus.ts:160,371), and assembleCharters derives a residual unit's node_id from a localeCompare-sorted file list (charterExtraction.ts:416-418). The repo already single-sources a code-unit comparator for exactly this reason (`compareCodeUnits` in src/shared/affinityArtifacts.ts, used by stableStringify's key sort and by contentCoherence.ts), and CLAUDE.md requires artifact array order to be a stable content-derived key — an environment-varying order churns the artifact content hash and cascades phantom staleness.

entries.rationale: Finding excluded by the intent checkpoint (filter or excluded scope).

finding.title: A directory-style glob with a trailing slash matches nothing once it contains a wildcard
finding.summary: pathMatchesPrefix strips trailing slashes from the entry path, so the non-wildcard directory form `vendor/` works. The wildcard branch of globMatches performs no such trimming: `vendor/**/` compiles to `^vendor/.*/$`, and file paths never end in `/`, so the pattern matches no file at all. A must_not_touch entry written in the directory form with a wildcard is therefore silently inert rather than protective — a fail-open, matching the same class as the primary finding but reachable through a different pattern shape.
evidence: src/shared/intent/pathScope.ts:22 - the non-glob path is normalized with `.replace(/\/+$/, "")`, deliberately tolerating a trailing slash on a directory entry.
src/shared/intent/pathScope.ts:31-33 - that trimming is only reached when the pattern contains neither `*` nor `?`; a wildcard pattern skips it entirely.
src/shared/intent/pathScope.ts:54 - the `$`-anchored regex built from `vendor/**/` requires a trailing `/` in the subject, which a file path never has.

finding.title: verifyFindingGrounding grounds a finding against files OUTSIDE the repo root
finding.summary: verifyFindingGrounding resolves a model-supplied affected_files[].path with isAbsolute(loc.path) ? loc.path : join(repoRoot, loc.path), so an absolute path (or a relative path containing ..) is read from anywhere on the machine. The grounding verdict is meant to be the tool's re-check of a cited span inside the audited repository; as written a worker can ground any claim by citing a file it controls outside the tree, and join() normalizes traversal segments so the escape is not even visible in the reason string.

evidence: src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:182 accepts an absolute cited path verbatim and joins relative ones without containment-checking the result against repoRoot.
The module docstring (lines 1-13) states the confirmed bit is the tool's re-check, never the model's word, yet the path being re-checked is entirely model-supplied.

finding.title: Planning's progress summary reports the pre-fold task count, understating the review set it actually persisted
finding.summary: runPlanningExecutor persists `audit_tasks: allReviewTasks` (planningExecutors.ts:241-244, 274), which is the canonicalized union of `enrichedAuditTasks` AND the folded `pendingRequeueTasks` — the module's own INV-PLAN-PERSIST-COMPLETE comment stresses that the whole merged list is the persisted set. Since this summary is the host's only textual signal about what planning produced, the drain's reported progress does not match the persisted artifact.

finding.title: splitBacklogEntries treats a `- **` line inside a fenced code block as a new backlog entry
finding.summary: The one shared definition of "a backlog entry" is a raw line scan (`/^- \*\*/`) with no fenced-code-block state. A backlog entry that quotes markdown in a ``` fence — which entries in this repo routinely do, since they show doc snippets and gate output — starts a phantom entry at that line. The consequences are not cosmetic: the roadmap generator derives a title from the phantom body and THROWS `entry has an UNTERMINATED bold title` if the quoted line has no closing `**` (blocking the pre-commit gate with a message pointing at the wrong defect), and the seek index emits an anchor at a line that is not an entry, which is exactly the "sends the reader to confidently wrong prose" failure the index says it prevents.

finding.title: outputJson silently prints "undefined" or throws for values JSON.stringify cannot serialize
finding.summary: outputJson passes an `unknown` value straight to JSON.stringify with no guard. JSON.stringify returns the JS value `undefined` for a top-level undefined, function, or symbol — console.log then writes the literal text "undefined" as the command's JSON output, producing machine output that no consumer can parse. For a circular structure or a BigInt it throws TypeError instead, surfacing as an unhandled crash from what reads like a formatting helper. Because the parameter is typed `unknown`, the type system offers no protection at any call site.
evidence: src/audit/cli/cliHelpers.ts:9 - `export function outputJson(data: unknown): void {` — the parameter is `unknown`, so any value at all is accepted with no narrowing or runtime check.

src/audit/cli/cliHelpers.ts:10 - `console.log(JSON.stringify(data, null, 2));` — the sole statement; the JSON.stringify result is neither checked for `undefined` nor wrapped in try/catch, so unserializable input yields the literal string "undefined" or an unhandled TypeError.
src/audit/cli/cliHelpers.ts:2 - the doc comment declares the helper is for "consistently formatted JSON command output", establishing that its output is expected to be parseable JSON on every call.
runtime:unit:src-audit: not_confirmed — Deterministic runtime command failed with exit code 1: npm test
reproduction: Call outputJson(undefined) — stdout receives the line `undefined`, which is not valid JSON.
Build a self-referential object (`const a: any = {}; a.self = a;`) and call outputJson(a) — JSON.stringify throws `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON` out of the helper.

finding.title: Unanswered clarification questions are erased from state on the same path that re-enters waiting_for_clarification
finding.summary: CONFIRMED and STRENGTHENED at HEAD. applyPlanClarificationResolution sets state.clarifications = [] unconditionally (line 2143) on the very branch that sets status to waiting_for_clarification because hasUnansweredClarification(state) is still true (lines 2138-2142), then persists at 2145. The waiting_for_clarification obligation (lines 3477-3492) re-emits handleWaitingForClarification, which resolves `state.clarifications ?? <file fallback> ?? []` (2155-2160) — an empty array is not nullish, so the fallback is short-circuited and clarificationPrompt renders a question list of zero entries. The consumed resolution was already archived at 2127, and the only repopulating writer is the host-handoff ingestion path (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/hostHandoff.ts:1291-1301), which runs only when a NEW worker question arrives — so the outstanding questions are unrecoverable and the run parks in a wait step that shows the operator nothing to answer. Severity/confidence stand at high/high; scope is exactly the partial-resolution path, no narrowing warranted.
evidence: src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2140 - `hasUnansweredClarification(state)` selects `waiting_for_clarification`, i.e. this branch is taken exactly when questions remain outstanding.
src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2143 - `state.clarifications = [];` runs unconditionally on that branch, before the persist at 2145.
src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2156 - `state.clarifications ?? (await readOptionalJsonFile(...)) ?? []` — `??` does not fall through on an empty array, so the persisted `[]` wins.

src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2168 - `clarificationPrompt(clarifications, resolutionPath, refusal)` renders the (empty) list; src/remediate/steps/prompts.ts:51 maps over it, producing no question sections.
src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2127 - the consumed resolution is renamed to `.consumed-*`, so the questions are not recoverable from the input either.

src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:3489 - the waiting_for_clarification obligation re-emits `handleWaitingForClarification(root, artifactsDir, s)` on the next derive, which is how the wiped state reaches the operator.
src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:433 - `hasUnansweredClarification` reads item.status only, so the paused items stay `needs_clarification` forever while their question payload is gone.

src/remediate/steps/dispatch/hostHandoff.ts:1301 - `nextState.clarifications = clarifications;` is the only repopulating writer, and it fires only on a fresh worker `needs_clarification` outcome, never as a recovery for the wipe.

finding.title: Outcomes/coverage contracts are TS interfaces only — their stated runtime invariants are unvalidated at the persistence boundary
finding.summary: Plan-side structures in this module are zod schemas that validate at load (`RemediationBlockSchema`, `RemediationPlanSchema`, `ItemSpecSchema`, `ClosingPlanSchema`, `RemediationHostHandoffRecordSchema`), but every structure written into `remediation-outcomes.json` — `CoverageLedger`, `CoverageLedgerEntry`, `RemediationOutcomeItem`, `OutcomeCoverageEntry`, `OutcomeCoverageLedger`, and `RemediationItemState` — is a bare TypeScript interface with no runtime schema. finding.title: VOI queue tie-break uses locale-dependent localeCompare, so the "stable content-derived order" it promises is not environment-stable
finding.summary: voiQueue breaks equal-VOI ties with a.request_id.localeCompare(b.request_id). localeCompare is collation-dependent: its result varies with the runtime's default locale and with the ICU data Node was built against (small-icu vs full-icu). The module header explicitly justifies the tie-break as content-derived precisely to avoid artifact-hash churn, but the chosen comparator makes the emitted order a function of the host environment rather than of content alone.

affected_files.quoted_text: return a.request_id.localeCompare(b.request_id);

finding.impact: Two runs on different machines (or the same machine under a different default locale / ICU build) can order equal-score requests differently. If that order reaches a persisted artifact, its content hash changes with no content change, cascading phantom staleness down the dependency DAG and triggering redundant downstream re-runs — exactly the failure the extractor-ordering invariant in CLAUDE.md exists to prevent.

finding.title: Stat-throttling test asserts nothing about stat calls — the named invariant is unverified
finding.summary: The test named "acquireLock does not call stat on every retry cycle" (lines 280-314) never observes stat at all: it holds a lock, times out, and then asserts the SAME boolean `timedOut` twice (lines 301 and 311). No spy, counter, or fs interception is installed, so the test passes identically whether stat is throttled, called every 50ms cycle, or never called. finding.title: Three tests bind acquireLock's token to `assert.doesNotReject`'s undefined return, then clean up with raw unlink instead of the token-checked release
finding.summary: At lines 161-165, 247-251, and 332-342 the tests write `const token = await assert.doesNotReject(() => acquireLock(...))` and then `void token`. `assert.doesNotReject` resolves to undefined, so `token` is never the acquired token — the comment at lines 172-173 acknowledges this. entries.title: An absent artifact_metadata manifest yields an empty stale set, so every derived artifact is treated as fresh
entries.rationale: Finding excluded by the intent checkpoint (filter or excluded scope).

finding.title: An absent artifact_metadata manifest yields an empty stale set, so every derived artifact is treated as fresh
finding.summary: computeStaleArtifacts gates all three of its detection phases on `if (metadata)` (lines 117, 194) — only the transitive closure at 213-246 runs unconditionally, and it can never seed itself because the stale set is empty. So when bundle.artifact_metadata is missing, the function returns an empty Set and the orchestrator concludes that nothing in the DAG is stale, no matter how far the on-disk artifacts have diverged from their inputs. This is the exact inverse of the adjacent CE-007 degrade at 108-115, which treats a merely OLD-SHAPE manifest as untrustworthy and marks every present DAG artifact stale. Losing the manifest entirely is a strictly weaker evidence state than holding an old-shape one, yet it produces the maximally trusting answer instead of the maximally conservative one. The comment at 106-107 states this as intended ("nothing to compare ⇒ nothing stale"), but the resulting integrity property is that a single deleted or truncated metadata file silently converts every downstream artifact — findings, report, coverage — into permanently-fresh stale data that no later invocation will ever re-derive.

finding.title: Present artifacts with no metadata entry are invisible to the dependency-hash pass and can only be caught by an absent upstream
finding.summary: The primary staleness comparison iterates `Object.entries(metadata.artifacts)` (line 118), i.e. the key space is the manifest, not the bundle. An artifact that is present on disk but has no manifest entry — written by an older tool version, restored from a backup, hand-repaired, or produced by a code path that skipped computeArtifactMetadata — is therefore never compared against its dependencies at all. The only path that can rescue it is the missing-upstream sweep at 194-211, and that sweep fires solely under the narrow condition that one of its declared upstreams is itself ABSENT from the bundle (line 202) and the downstream has no metadata entry (204-206). If all upstreams are present, an entry-less artifact is silently classified fresh, and the transitive closure cannot reach it either, because nothing seeded the set. The consequence for the audit loop is that a stale, unrecorded artifact satisfies its obligation and its content feeds synthesis as if it were current.

entries.title: Slice-protected edges suppress transitive staleness on an ordering assumption held only by a comment in another module
entries.rationale: Finding excluded by the intent checkpoint (filter or excluded scope).

finding.title: Slice-protected edges suppress transitive staleness on an ordering assumption held only by a comment in another module
finding.summary: In the closure loop, a downstream is NOT marked stale through an upstream edge when the downstream's stored entry recorded a slice for that edge and a projection is registered (lines 235-241). Correctness of that suppression rests entirely on the assumption stated in the comment at 229-234: that every slice-projected upstream's obligation runs BEFORE the downstream's in the PRIORITY array of nextStep.ts, and that staleness is re-derived on each drain iteration so the per-edge slice compare fires after the upstream re-derives. Nothing in this module — or, as far as this file expresses, in any mechanical check — verifies that ordering. If a future edge is registered in dependencySlices.ts whose upstream obligation sits at or after the downstream's in PRIORITY, the downstream is skipped pre-emptively here and its own recorded slice is compared against a bundle in which the upstream has not yet re-derived, so the slice still matches its previous value and the downstream is declared fresh over superseded upstream content. The failure is silent and produces no staleness record. Per the repo's own auditor-agnostic rule, an invariant of this kind should be enforced (e.g. a contract test asserting every slice-projected pair's PRIORITY ordering), not documented.
evidence: src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts:235-241 — `const entry = metadata?.artifacts[downstream]; if (entry?.dependency_slices?.[upstream] !== undefined && hasDependencySliceProjection(downstream, upstream)) { continue; }` — the edge is skipped without any check of relative obligation order.

src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts:163-178 — the direct (non-transitive) slice compare likewise substitutes the slice for the whole-hash + revision disjunction, so once the transitive mark is suppressed the whole-hash fallback is unavailable to catch the divergence.

finding.title: Cached contributions carry no shape/tool version, so a change to PerFileGraphContribution silently reuses old-shaped entries
finding.summary: The persisted record written by writeGraphEdgeCache (src/audit/orchestrator/graphEdgeCache.ts:28-33) is exactly {path_lookup_hash, entries} (src/audit/extractors/graph.ts:104-107) — there is no schema_version, tool version, or extractor-logic key. finding.title: A duplicate task_id silently discards an entire chunk of files instead of merging or reporting
finding.summary: addTaskBlock dedupes purely on the derived task_id string. In the normal-chunk loop (src/audit/orchestrator/taskBuilder.ts:172-189) a chunk whose id is already in `seen` is skipped without pushing anything, and in the oversized-file loop (192-197) the same `continue` fires. finding.title: The synthetic remainder unit id is a lossy path sanitization that can collide across distinct files
finding.summary: buildRemainderBlocks derives a fallback unit id as `review:${path.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/g, "-")}` (src/audit/orchestrator/taskBuilder.ts:312). The substitution is many-to-one: 'src/a/b.ts', 'src/a-b.ts' and 'src/a.b.ts' all map to 'review:src-a-b-ts'. finding.summary: The CE-007 fail-safe deliberately distrusts an OLDER manifest, but both gates are written as `>=`, so a manifest written by a NEWER schema version is classified `previousIsCurrent` / `bundleIsCurrent` and is fully trusted: its per-artifact entries are carried verbatim (line 138), and result_baselines, coverage_element_baselines, git_history_baseline and intent_baseline are copied onto the output manifest — which is then re-stamped with the OLDER METADATA_SCHEMA_VERSION (line 203). finding.title: A dependency cycle is silently broken, emitting a dependent before its dependency and freezing that dep at a stale/zero revision
finding.summary: computeDependencyFirstOrder's DFS marks in-progress nodes in `temporary` and, on re-entry, simply returns (line 33) with no cycle signal. If ARTIFACT_DEPENDS_ON_MAP ever contains a cycle (it is hand-maintained data, and the file's own comments describe real staleness ping-pong between runtime_validation and synthesis), the fold still produces an order — but one in which at least one artifact is emitted before a dependency it needs. computeArtifactMetadata then reads that dependency's revision from `artifacts[dependencyName]` (not yet populated) and falls back to `usablePrevious?.artifacts[dep]?.revision ?? 0`, recording a stale or zero upstream revision into dependency_revisions. The topological invariant the whole metadata contract rests on is unenforced: there is no throw, no diagnostic, and no marker on the manifest.

finding.title: computeArtifactStateSignature returns the constant "no-metadata", so two distinct metadata-less bundle states are indistinguishable to the cycle detector

finding.title: A persisted-but-invalid value wedges every mutate() with no in-band repair path
finding.summary: validate() runs only on the write side (persist), never on parse. If a value that passes parse() but fails validate() is already on disk (written by an older schema, a hand edit, or a replace() call whose validate was added later), every subsequent mutate() aborts: the callback's result is validated, throws, and the whole read-modify-write fails before any write. State transitions stop permanently until a caller reaches for replace(), which is documented as the recovery escape but is itself validated too, so the only recovery is out-of-band file surgery.

src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts:111 - mutate() routes every non-SKIP_WRITE result through persist(), so a value the callback merely passed through unchanged still fails validation and aborts the transition.
src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts:68-75 - replace() is documented as the corrupt-value recovery path but also goes through persist(), so it is subject to the same validate() rejection.

finding.title: Persisted `complete` status short-circuits state derivation, so staleness can never invalidate a finished run
finding.summary: decideNextStep returns early on bundle.audit_state?.status === "complete" (lines 121-128) and returns the persisted audit_state verbatim without ever calling deriveAuditState. Because staleness (and therefore obligation re-derivation) is computed only inside deriveAuditState, a run whose artifacts were persisted as complete stays complete even when upstream inputs (repo files, manifest, structure artifacts) have since changed and the dependency DAG would mark downstream artifacts stale. DecideNextStepOptions.emitStaleness (lines 104-113) is therefore inert for any bundle already marked complete.

finding.title: Nested-tree guard is case-sensitive, so a differently-cased root still mints a phantom .audit-tools tree
finding.summary: auditToolsDir() rejects a nested artifact tree by testing resolve(root).split(sep).includes('.audit-tools') — an exact, case-sensitive string match. finding.title: Published worker schemas silently drop the zod cross-field refinement on line ranges
finding.summary: The worker-facing JSON Schemas are generated from zod via zodToJsonSchema, which cannot express .refine() predicates. finding.title: readStaleLockToken TOCTOU lets a stealer unlink a fresh successor lock

finding.title: releaseLock can delete a successor's lock if heartbeat lapsed
finding.summary: releaseLock does a non-atomic check-then-delete: it readFile's the lock content, verifies it equals our ownerToken, and only then unlink()s. If our heartbeat has missed STALE_LOCK_MS (best-effort utimes, event-loop stall, slow FS), the lock is judged stale by another waiter and stolen between our readFile and unlink. The intervening steal unlinks and re-creates the path with the new holder's token; our already-passed token check then proceeds to unlink the successor's fresh lock. The successor continues running its critical section believing it holds the lock.
finding.impact: A legitimately held lock belonging to a different holder can be deleted by us, letting the original holder and a new acquirer both think they hold the lock — concurrent mutation of the guarded artifact.

finding.summary: tests/remediate/host-handoff.test.ts:516 derives the repo root with `resolve(new URL("../..", import.meta.url).pathname.replace(/^\/(\p{L}:)/u, "$1"))` — a hand-written Windows drive-letter strip on a URL pathname. finding.title: Self-asserting tests that exercise no system under test (object literals asserted against themselves)
finding.summary: Several tests build a local object literal and then assert its own fields, so they can never fail regardless of the code they claim to cover. tests/shared/contractPipeline-types.test.ts is almost entirely this shape: every `it` declares an `ImplementationDAGNode` / `SeamNegotiationRecord` / `ObligationEntry` literal and asserts the literal back (e.g. `expect(node.id).toBe("N-001")` at line 39, `expect(entry.priority).toBe(1)` at line 145, and the JSON.stringify/JSON.parse round-trip at lines 101-109 which tests `JSON`, not the contract). The only non-vacuous assertion in the file is the version constant at line 113. The same pattern closes tests/shared/clauseInterpreter.test.ts: `IntentCheckpoint without constraint_clauses is still valid` (lines 189-201) asserts `!("constraint_clauses" in checkpoint)` on an object it just wrote without that key, and `IntentCheckpoint constraint_clauses entries carry ...` (lines 203-218) asserts `typeof entry.text === "string"` on its own literal. These names promise contract coverage the assertions do not provide, so a real regression in the type contract (a field removed, a schema tightened) leaves the suite green while reading as covered.

reproduction: Delete or rename any optional field on ImplementationDAGNode / ObligationEntry in src/shared/types/contractPipeline.ts

finding.title: validateFinding's required-field set is split between requireKeys and an out-of-band evidence check
finding.summary: validateFinding declares its required keys in one place (requireKeys at lines 27-36: id, title, category, severity, confidence, lens, summary, affected_files) but then enforces a ninth mandatory field out of band: lines 73-80 reject a finding whose evidence is missing or empty, with an explicitly-passed "error" severity. A reader (or a producer building a finding to spec) who consults the requireKeys list — the obvious declaration of the contract — will conclude evidence is optional and emit a finding this validator rejects. Either evidence belongs in the requireKeys list with its non-empty constraint stated alongside, or the split needs a comment explaining why it is deliberate; as written the required-field contract has two homes.

finding.title: shouldLogPollAttempt is regex-extracted and eval'd with new Function instead of being imported
finding.summary: STANDS. The extraction mechanism is unchanged at HEAD: tests/audit/release-contract.test.ts:173-175 still reconstructs the helper via `new Function(...)` from regex-extracted source text rather than importing scripts/poll-log-throttle.mjs, whose ESM export `export { POLL_LOG_EVERY_N_ATTEMPTS, shouldLogPollAttempt };` (scripts/poll-log-throttle.mjs:21) is already available. finding.title: The throttle behavior test rebuilds the helper from a regex-extracted string via new Function instead of importing the module it claims to test
finding.summary: Found while verifying MNT-TA11-001; this is the sharpest instance of the same class and deserves its own entry because it is a correctness defect, not only brittleness. `scripts/poll-log-throttle.mjs` is a pure ES module that explicitly exports both `POLL_LOG_EVERY_N_ATTEMPTS` and `shouldLogPollAttempt`, and its header comment states that unit tests import the throttle from there. The test does not import it. It reads the file as text, extracts the constant and the function body with two regexes, concatenates them into a `new Function(...)` and exercises THAT reconstruction. Consequences: (1) the shipped export binding is never exercised — deleting or renaming the export on line 21 of the helper leaves this test green, so the release script could fail to import a symbol the suite just "verified"; (2) the body regex `/function shouldLogPollAttempt\([^)]*\) \{[\s\S]*?\n\}/` is non-greedy to the first column-zero `}`, so adding any nested block (an `if (...) {` … `}` at the top level of the body) silently truncates the extracted source and the test fails with a syntax error from `new Function` rather than a meaningful assertion; (3) the same fragile pattern is duplicated in two places (lines 129 and 158-160), so the extraction grammar must be maintained twice. The fix is a one-line `import { POLL_LOG_EVERY_N_ATTEMPTS, shouldLogPollAttempt } from "../../scripts/poll-log-throttle.mjs"`, which makes the purity assertions on lines 168-171 redundant against real behavior and removes the reconstruction entirely.

finding.summary: src/audit/validation/artifacts.ts:376-380 has the public validator emit `[artifact-bundle validation] N issue(s)` directly to `process.stderr` before returning its issue list. finding.title: Alias-only indirection layers (`pushIssue`, `defaultAnchorRunner`, `ANCHOR_TIMEOUT_MS`, and the anchorGrounding re-export shim) exist solely to keep old names alive
finding.summary: Four separate one-line aliases add a name without adding behaviour. artifacts.ts:10-16 defines `pushIssue` as a verbatim forwarder to the shared `pushValidationIssue`, used 20+ times, so a reader must resolve two hops to learn the issue shape. anchorGrounding.ts:39-42 re-exports `isAllowedAnchorCommand`/`ANCHOR_ALLOWLIST`/`GIT_READONLY_SUBCOMMANDS` with an explicit comment that its purpose is to keep existing import sites working after the implementation moved to shared; :45 aliases `ALLOWLISTED_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS` to `ANCHOR_TIMEOUT_MS`; :61 aliases the shared runner type; :68 wraps `runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand` as `defaultAnchorRunner` with a comment saying the alias exists so 'injected test runners and callers are unchanged'. Under the repo's ideal-code-over-compatibility rule these are compatibility shims for a single-consumer tree: each gives the same concept two names, so a grep for the real symbol misses the audit-side usages and the shared/audit boundary reads as a real seam when it is not.
evidence: src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts:39-41 comment: 'Re-export the allowlist authority so existing audit-code import sites (`../validation/anchorGrounding.js`) keep working'.
src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts:66-68 comment: 'Exposed under the local name so injected test runners and callers are unchanged.'
src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts:45 `export const ANCHOR_TIMEOUT_MS = ALLOWLISTED_EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS;` — a second public name for one constant.
src/audit/validation/artifacts.ts:10-16 `function pushIssue(issues, path, message) { pushValidationIssue(issues, path, message); }` — parameter-for-parameter forwarder.
runtime:unit:src-audit: not_confirmed — Deterministic runtime command failed with exit code 1: npm test
reproduction: Grep the tree for `runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand` or `pushValidationIssue`: the audit-side call sites do not appear, because they are reached through the local aliases.
A maintainer changing the shared runner's signature must additionally reconcile three audit-local names that describe the same thing.

finding.title: Architecture invariants in git-history-mining.test.ts are asserted by regex over source text, so they are both fragile and over-broad
finding.summary: Three 'F6 inv' tests enforce structural boundaries by reading src/audit/extractors/gitHistory.ts as a string and pattern-matching it. The import test only inspects lines that individually match /^\s*import\b/ or /\bfrom\s+["']/, so a multi-line import whose module specifier sits on its own line is silently exempt; the anti-mutation test forbids the literal token `register.items` anywhere in the file, which would also fire on an unrelated local variable named register, and forbids `.graphs.imports|calls|references|routes` even inside a comment. These invariants are real, but expressed as text matching they will fail on a harmless reformat and pass on a real violation written slightly differently.

finding.title: envelopePayload's parameter type contradicts its body, and readContractArtifact never validates the envelope
finding.summary: readContractArtifact casts whatever JSON is on disk to ContractPipelineArtifactEnvelope with no structural check, even though isEnvelope() exists in the same module as the canonical predicate. envelopePayload then declares its parameter as ContractPipelineArtifactEnvelope|null but internally re-tests isEnvelope() and, when false, returns the argument itself as the payload — so the declared type is a lie the body works around. A reader cannot tell from the signature that a bare (non-enveloped) payload is an accepted input, and the compiler cannot help when the two paths diverge.

finding.title: Three files re-implement the hermetic temp-git-repo helper with subtly different semantics
finding.summary: region-merge-writescope.test.ts, source-grounded-citation.test.ts and n-r13-document-phase-dissolved.test.ts each define a local git() wrapper over spawnSyncHidden plus repo-setup code (init, config user.email/user.name, add). finding.title: optionalImport swallows every import error, so an unrelated failure reads as 'retired import no longer resolves'
finding.summary: optionalImport (lines 58-64) catches all throwables and returns null. It is used both to assert presence (lines 85, 139, 143) and, at line 200, to assert ABSENCE: retiredDeepImport !== null is treated as proof the retired deep import audit-tools/shared/types/attributionContract is gone. Any failure inside that module's transitive graph - a syntax error, a missing peer, a stale dist artifact that throws on load - also yields null and the check silently passes. The absence assertion cannot distinguish 'removed' from 'present but broken', which is precisely the state a stale build leaves behind, and the same helper's presence checks degrade to a generic 'schema is missing' violation with no underlying error text to debug from.

finding.summary: Four distinct temp-dir idioms appear in this file set for the same need. analyzer-seam.test.ts repeats a mkdtemp + try/finally + rm block four times (two mkdtemps per block); analyzer-consent-offer.test.ts builds its own RM_DIRS registry plus an afterEach reaper; audit-extractors-invariants.test.ts uses a shared helper `withTempDir` from tests/audit/helpers/withTempDir.mjs; the wrapper suites use `withTempRepo` from the wrapper harness, while audit-code-wrapper-cli-surface.test.ts still hand-rolls mkdtemp/try/finally three times. finding.title: Ordering in git.ts and dedupe.ts uses locale-sensitive localeCompare while the sibling deterministic module uses an explicit codepoint comparator
finding.summary: mineGitHistory sorts churn, authorship, and co-change tie-breaks with String.prototype.localeCompare, and mergeAffectedFiles sorts affected files the same way. localeCompare is ICU/locale-dependent, so the tie-break order of these persisted, content-hashed artifacts can differ between environments. modularity.ts deliberately avoids exactly this by defining compareNodeIds for its determinism guarantee, so the codebase carries two contradictory conventions for 'stable order'.

finding.title: Flake-baseline test drives an untyped .mjs script module, so contract drift is invisible to the test typecheck gate
finding.summary: tests/shared/parallel-flake-baseline.test.ts is TypeScript but imports its entire subject - twelve symbols including updateFlakeBaseline, mergeObservations and classifyFailures - from ../../scripts/shared/vitest-timing-reporter.mjs (lines 18-31). finding.title: flowCoverage emits completed_lenses in observation order, not a stable content-derived order
finding.summary: buildFlowCoverage accumulates matched lenses into a Set in the order they are encountered while walking flow paths and each coverage record's completed_lenses, then materialises the artifact field with a bare spread. The resulting array order is therefore a function of upstream traversal and of the order in which each coverage record happens to list its own completed lenses, not of the flow's declared concern order or any sort. Under the repo's stable-array-order invariant this is a latent content-hash churn source: an unchanged audit state whose upstream record order shifts re-hashes flow_coverage and cascades phantom staleness to its dependents. required_lenses is safe by contrast because it preserves the declared concerns order. Sorting completed_lenses, or emitting it as required_lenses filtered by membership, removes the dependency on observation order at no behavioural cost — status is computed with includes() and is order-insensitive.
evidence: src/audit/orchestrator/flowCoverage.ts:34 - const completed = new Set<string>() accumulates in insertion (observation) order

src/audit/orchestrator/flowCoverage.ts:48 - const completed_lenses = [...completed] materialises that order directly into the artifact with no sort
src/audit/orchestrator/flowCoverage.ts:50 - status uses required.every(lens => completed_lenses.includes(lens)), confirming order carries no semantics and a sort would be behaviour-preserving

finding.title: Test-output path attribution rests on an unanchored regex plus four-way suffix matching with no documented bound
finding.summary: extractImplicatedPaths applies a broad unanchored regex to raw test output and treats any dotted token as a candidate path, then blockResolvedItemsOnCombinedFailure matches items with a four-clause suffix test (tf === ip || tf.endsWith('/'+ip) || ip.endsWith('/'+tf) || tf.endsWith(ip) || ip.endsWith(tf)). finding.title: Release contract tests assert on source-text regexes instead of behavior, coupling the gate to formatting
finding.summary: The finding STANDS at HEAD, unchanged in severity and confidence, and its scope is WIDER than the original 83-149 span: the source-text-pin pattern runs the whole file, not just the release-helper test. Every cited pin exists verbatim. The mechanism is confirmed: these are regexes over the source TEXT of scripts the test never executes or imports, so (a) a purely cosmetic edit to the target script (prettier reflow, renaming a local, swapping a ternary for an if, moving an argument to its own line) turns the release gate red with no behavior change, and (b) the behavior can regress while the matched text survives — asserting that `run(npm, ["run", "verify:checks"])` appears in the file proves nothing about whether that call is reachable, guarded, or ordered before the tag. The file's own comment at lines 89-94 documents that exact miss (a previous pin "was satisfied by the word 'verify:release' appearing in a comment") and the remedy chosen was a tighter text pin rather than an executable assertion, so the class was acknowledged and not fixed. The most brittle instance is line 323, which pins the exact brace-and-whitespace layout of an if-block in a different file (`/if \(counts\.failed > 0\) \{\s*process\.exitCode = 1;\s*\}/`): reformatting `install-host-assets.mjs`, or replacing the if with an equivalent guard, fails the audit suite. Roughly 60 such text pins across ten tests must now be maintained in lockstep with the formatting of eight scripts, two workflows and three docs. Narrowing note: the two tests that read structured data rather than text (lines 30-40 and 326-332, which `JSON.parse` package.json and knip.json and compare parsed values) are NOT part of the defect and should be excluded from any remediation scope — they assert the real contract value. Recommended disposition: STANDS at high/high, with affected span widened from 83-149 to 83-324 and the JSON-parsing tests explicitly carved out.

finding.title: prefixValidationIssues' idempotency guard cannot distinguish an already-prefixed path from a coincidental match
finding.summary: The guard skips prefixing whenever an issue path equals `prefix` or starts with `${prefix}.`. Nested contracts here reuse segment names across levels (findingsReport builds paths such as `findings.0.theme_id` and `work_blocks.0.finding_ids.0`), so an unprefixed issue whose first segment happens to equal the caller's prefix is silently left unprefixed and reports the wrong location. The docstring presents the guard as unconditionally safe ("safe to call on a mix of already-prefixed and unprefixed issues") while the check is textual and therefore only heuristic — a maintainer has no signal that the invariant is not actually established.

          ? issue.path
          : `${prefix}.${issue.path}`,

finding.title: Backslash-path test never compares against the forward-slash result it names
finding.summary: tests/remediate/intake-risk-signal.test.ts:47 is titled "treats Windows backslash paths the same as forward-slash", but its body computes only the backslash variant and asserts `tier === "high"` plus `matched_path_risks.length > 0` — it never computes the forward-slash spelling, so it cannot detect the sameness it claims. finding.title: Cycle assertions mutate the value under test with in-place sort and compare arrays by default string coercion
finding.summary: detectCyclicSeamObligations results are asserted via `cycles[0].members.sort()`, which sorts the returned array in place — the assertion mutates the object it is inspecting, so any later assertion in the same test observes reordered data and a genuine ordering regression in the producer is masked rather than caught. The two-cycle test compounds this by mapping each cycle through an in-place sort and then calling `.sort()` on the resulting array of arrays, which compares them by JavaScript's default string coercion of the nested arrays; that happens to order ['A','B'] before ['C','D'] here but is not a stated or stable contract, so the test is pinned to an accident of the fixture's letters. A non-mutating sort of a copy, or an order-insensitive matcher, would say the same thing without either hazard.
evidence: tests/remediate/cyclic-seam-resolution.test.ts:69 — `expect(cycles[0].members.sort()).toEqual(["A", "B"])`

finding.title: The spacing 'regression lock' greps nextStep.ts source text with an obfuscated, near-vacuous pair of assertions
finding.summary: MNT-d86014de is checked by reading src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts as raw text and asserting two things about it. The negative assertion is written as `'or `none`"'.replace(/ /g, "")`, a runtime string transform that hides the literal being searched for and forces every reader to evaluate it by hand. The positive assertion, `expect(nextStepSrc).toContain('or `none`')`, matches anywhere in a multi-thousand-line file, so any unrelated occurrence keeps it green even if the intent-checkpoint prompt regressed. Neither assertion renders the prompt or exercises the code path that produced the bug, so the lock does not bind the behavior it was written for.

finding.title: CRLF normalization is ad hoc: three copies of normalizeNewlines plus scattered inline replaces, applied inconsistently
finding.summary: `normalizeNewlines` is defined identically in three modules (io.mjs:113, legacy.mjs:5, install-hosts.mjs:58) and the same `.replace(/\r\n/g, '\n')` is additionally inlined at install-hosts.mjs:104 (path separators), 603, 604, 916, 917, 1056, 1057, 1101. The duplication has already produced divergence: the installed-skill freshness checks normalize both sides (install-hosts.mjs:916-917 and 1056-1057) while the installed-prompt checks compare raw strings (install-hosts.mjs:901-903 and 1046-1047), so a checkout with CRLF prompt assets reports a permanently stale prompt but a fresh skill. A single shared normalizer would make the policy one decision instead of nine.
evidence: Identical `function normalizeNewlines(value) { return value.replace(/\r\n/g, '\n'); }` at io.mjs:113-115, legacy.mjs:5-7, install-hosts.mjs:58-60.
Prompt compare is unnormalized (install-hosts.mjs:1046-1049) while skill compare directly below it is normalized (install-hosts.mjs:1056-1059).

finding.title: writeCodex install profile flag is unreachable, keeping a whole dead Codex asset path alive
finding.summary: `writeCodex` is listed in INSTALL_PROFILE_FLAGS (line 134) but no entry in INSTALL_HOST_DEFINITIONS sets it — the codex host profile is `{ writeAgents: true }` (line 163-165), and getInstallProfile only ORs flags from those profiles (line 336). finding.title: riskSignal.ts bundles four unrelated concerns in one 564-line module, including a relocated lean-light-review verdict parser
finding.summary: The module simultaneously owns (1) the risk-tier vocabulary and combinator, (2) two consumer-facing dials (`adversarialDepthForTier`, `roundTripGranularityForTier`) that map a tier onto pipeline behavior, (3) the intake computation plus its configurable pattern/keyword tables and the escalate-on-evidence derivations, (4) on-disk persistence of the signal, and (5) an unrelated host-verdict parser for the lean light review (`interpretLeanLightReviewVerdict` and its own schema-version constant), whose own comment records it was relocated here from a retired module. finding.impact: Changes to any one of the five concerns force a reader through the whole file; the transplanted verdict parser in particular has no discoverable home from its own name.

finding.title: Four different module-loading conventions across six sibling test files in tests/audit
finding.summary: The six suites in this part load the code under test four different ways: static ESM import (git-history-mining, graph-framework-routes), top-level `await import` bound to a destructured const (graph-external-analyzers, graph-manifest-edges, graph-signal-consumers), and a bespoke `importSourceModule("src/...ts")` helper (graph-python-imports). Shared types are likewise reached through two different specifiers for the same module — `audit-tools/shared` and `../../src/shared/index.js` — inside the same directory, and graph-external-analyzers.test.ts uses both idioms in one file. The importSourceModule route is the costly one: it returns untyped values, so the whole graph-python-imports suite runs without the typecheck the repo's check:tests gate is supposed to provide, and the file has to re-declare `type PythonFromImportTarget` by hand (line 8) to get any shape back.

finding.summary: The run-log assertions (lines 327-346) locate the second and third invocations by `findIndex` over event ordinals and then use `const endOfSecondInvocation = thirdInvocationStart > 0 ? thirdInvocationStart : events.length;`. finding.title: The two git-spawn evaluators in disposition.ts duplicate their whole error/exit-code contract
finding.summary: evaluateVcsIgnored (disposition.ts:207-252) and evaluateTrackedFiles (:265-306) are structurally the same function: try/catch around one spawnSync with cwd/encoding/maxBuffer 256MiB/windowsHide, an identical result.error branch that special-cases ENOENT, an exit-status branch, a NUL-split of stdout into a Set, and an identical stderr-first-line extraction `(result.stderr ?? "").trim().split(/\r?\n/, 1)[0] ?? ""` for the failure reason. Only the argv and the accepted status set (0|1 vs 0) genuinely differ. The duplicated pieces are the ones that must not drift — the maxBuffer ceiling, the ENOENT wording, and the never-throw guarantee the doc comments promise — so a fix applied to one evaluator (say, raising maxBuffer for a huge repo) is a change the other silently does not receive. The same duplication continues one level up in applyVcsIgnoreRule (:350-417) and applyUntrackedRule (:431-494), which each re-implement the root guard and the VCS_IGNORED_MAX_SHARE share guard around a shared skippedRule/applyRuleExclusions core.

finding.title: evaluateAutonomousFinding derives a synthetic spec for the tier check but passes the raw (possibly undefined) spec to the change-kind check
finding.summary: The function builds `effectiveSpec` — a minimal ItemSpec whose `concrete_change` is the finding prose — specifically so the risk classifier still sees the finding text when no spec exists, then calls `classifyFindingRisk(finding, effectiveSpec)`. One line later it calls `classifyChangeKind(finding, spec)` with the ORIGINAL possibly-undefined `spec`, not `effectiveSpec`. The two halves of a single verdict therefore run on different inputs, and the reason for the asymmetry is documented nowhere. A maintainer reading the function cannot tell whether this is deliberate (changeText already folds in the same prose) or an oversight, which is precisely the ambiguity that makes safety-gate code hard to change.

finding.title: The autonomous gate's approval predicate double-encodes allowlist membership
finding.summary: `evaluateAutonomousFinding` computes `approved = tierSafe && kind.allowlisted && SAFE_CHANGE_KINDS.has(kind.change_kind)`, but `ChangeKindClassification.allowlisted` is itself documented as "whether the kind is positively on the fail-closed allowlist" and is hand-set to a literal true/false at each of the six return sites in `classifyChangeKind`. finding.title: Two independent cycle detectors over the same module-dependency graph
finding.summary: cyclicSeamResolution.ts implements Kahn's algorithm plus a hand-rolled union-find to detect and group module cycles, while phaseCut.ts independently detects cycles with a memoized DFS that sets has_cycle. Both read the same conceptual graph (module -> modules it needs / depends_on) but use different node shapes (SeamObligationNode.needs vs PhaseCutModule.depends_on) and different edge-normalization rules (cyclicSeamResolution ignores unknown refs but keeps self-edges; derivePhaseCut drops self-edges explicitly). Two detectors with divergent normalization means a graph can be reported cyclic by one and acyclic by the other, and any future fix has to be found and applied twice.
evidence: src/remediate/contractPipeline/cyclicSeamResolution.ts:60-143 — detectCyclicSeamObligations: Kahn drain + union-find grouping over SeamObligationNode.needs; unknown refs skipped (line 77) but a self-edge is counted as in-degree.

finding.summary: The comment at lines 41-44 states the reason explicitly: audit integration tests spawn real subprocesses and can run for over a minute, 'Remediate/shared unit tests finish far under it.' finding.title: The tsc diagnostic regex cannot match a Windows absolute path (drive-letter colon)
finding.summary: runTsc parses diagnostics with /^([^:]+)\((\d+),\d+\):\s+(error\s+TS\d+:.*)$/ (syntaxResolutionExecutor.ts:101). The `[^:]+` path group stops at the first colon, so any diagnostic emitted with an absolute Windows path (`C:/repo/src/x.ts(3,5): error TS2345: ...`) never matches and is dropped without any signal — the run then looks like an unparseable-output or empty-findings run. This is a platform-baked assumption in a project whose conventions require OS-agnostic core logic.

finding.summary: Every extractor in this set orders its emitted arrays with String.prototype.localeCompare, whose collation depends on the runtime's default locale and ICU build rather than on content alone. fileInventory.ts:60 sorts repo_manifest.files with a.path.localeCompare(b.path) directly beneath a long comment explaining that this sort exists to keep re-extraction byte-identical and prevent phantom staleness cascading down the dependency DAG; the same locale-sensitive comparator is used for docsDigest.ts:104,135, flows.ts:75,211, dataStateCoupling.ts:83,98, commentDecomposition.ts:300,351,378,411,414, designAssessment.ts:224,248,271,334 and browserExtension.ts:459. Two runs on machines with different default locales (or a small-icu vs full-icu Node) can therefore emit differently ordered arrays for identical content, which is exactly the content-hash churn the fileInventory comment says the sort was added to prevent. A code-unit comparator (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0) would make ordering a pure function of content; single-sourcing it as one shared comparator would also stop the 15+ call sites from drifting.

finding.title: readPackageVersion test reimplements the function inline and asserts against its own copy
finding.summary: CONFIRMED at HEAD, stands as filed at high/high. The test 'readPackageVersion logs to stderr on JSON parse error and returns null (OBS-9335faf6)' never reaches the production symbol: readPackageVersion is a module-private function in src/audit/io/toolingManifest.ts (declared, not exported, at line 51) and the test file imports only buildToolingManifest. The test writes a broken package.json into a temp dir and then runs a hand-written duplicate of the read/parse/stderr-log logic in its own body, asserting on that duplicate. Any regression in the real implementation - a removed stderr write, a changed message prefix, a throw instead of returning null - leaves this test green. The affected scope is exactly one test (lines 333-382) and does not widen: the file's other tests do call real code. The correct fix is to make the path reachable (export readPackageVersion, or inject the package root so buildToolingManifest can be pointed at a temp dir) rather than to keep the duplicate, since the comment at 336-339 records the substitution as a technique and will otherwise be copied.

finding.title: Several audit-cli invariant tests assert only JS builtins or a local re-implementation, never the code they name
finding.summary: audit-cli-invariants.test.ts contains a cluster of tests that carry an invariant id and a source-file claim in their name, but whose assertions never reach that source. INV-audit-cli-09 asserts only Array.isArray(null)/Array.isArray([]) — pure language semantics, with the real guard in importExternalAnalyzerCommand.ts unexercised. INV-audit-cli-12 defines a local checkMutex() that 'mirrors the fixed logic in cmdIngestResults' and asserts against that copy, so the shipped mutex can be deleted with the test still green. INV-audit-cli-03's second test asserts a locally built Set does not contain 'partial'. INV-audit-cli-10 asserts a locally built Set contains its own members. INV-audit-cli-13 asserts typeof runAuditStep === 'function' and then literally expect(true, ...). These are green-by-construction: they cost maintenance and reading time while providing no regression signal, and they read as coverage to a future maintainer.

finding.title: syntax-resolution tests mutate process-global PATH and stderr with a lossy restore
finding.summary: tests/audit/syntax-resolution.test.ts saves and restores two process globals by hand. The PATH test (lines 141-163) does `const originalPath = process.env.PATH; process.env.PATH = ""; ... process.env.PATH = originalPath;` — when PATH is unset the restore assigns undefined, which Node coerces to the literal string "undefined" rather than deleting the key, so the environment is not returned to its prior state. The two stderr tests (266-270, 302-306) monkey-patch process.stderr.write with a cast-through-unknown call shim, restored only in a finally block; any throw inside the patched region between the assignment and the try leaves the global patched for the rest of the worker. Both patterns are repeated rather than centralized, so each new test in this file re-derives the same fragile save/restore.

finding.title: Predicates are collapsed into toBeTruthy/toBeFalsy, so failures report 'expected false to be truthy' with no values
finding.summary: Across all six files the dominant assertion shape is `expect(<boolean expression>, "message").toBeTruthy()` — e.g. `expect(!taskPaths.includes("src/gen.ts"), ...)`, `expect(markdown.includes(finding.id), ...)`, `expect(evidence.includes("e1"), ...)`, `expect(testSuite.includes("20.19.2"), ...).toBeFalsy()`. Vitest can only print `expected false to be truthy`; the actual array, markdown, or workflow text never reaches the failure output, so every failure requires re-running with an ad-hoc console log to learn what the value was. The equivalent matchers (`expect(taskPaths).not.toContain(...)`, `expect(markdown).toContain(finding.id)`, `expect(evidence).toEqual([...])`) carry the same intent and print both sides. Several call sites already work around the loss by interpolating the value into the message string (planning-executors 196-198), which is the tell.

finding.title: isRecord admits arrays, so the Record<string, unknown> narrowing is weaker than its name and the `as T` cast is unchecked
finding.summary: isRecord (lines 52-54) only checks typeof value === 'object' && value !== null, which is true for arrays. A JSON line such as [] therefore narrows to Record<string, unknown>; it fails the event comparison today only incidentally (obj.event is undefined), so the guard's correctness rests on the caller's extra check rather than the guard. Both helpers then cast the value with `obj as T` without validating any field of T beyond `event`, so a malformed event line is handed to test assertions typed as fully-formed T. For a shared test helper this makes downstream failures surface as confusing property-access errors instead of a clear parse/shape error at the boundary.
evidence: Lines 52-54: function isRecord(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown> { return typeof value === "object" && value !== null; } — Array.isArray is not excluded.
Line 20: return [obj as T]; and line 43: return obj as T; — unchecked widening to the caller-supplied generic.

The helper exists in this very file (line 886-888), so the divergence is an oversight rather than a policy: two copies of one matching rule that have already drifted. Practically, an invariant id containing regex metacharacters (e.g. "INV-A(1)" or "INV.*") either changes the match semantics or makes `new RegExp` throw out of a gate that is documented to return issues rather than fail. The word-boundary containment rule should be one shared helper used by both call sites.

finding.title: classifyFindingRisk's lens regexes cannot match any canonical lens value
finding.summary: classifyFindingRisk (src/remediate/steps/stepUtils.ts:110-143) tiers a finding by regex-matching `finding.lens`. The safe test is /\b(style|format|lint|typo|whitespace|cosmetic|config)\b/ and the breaking test is /\b(compat|api[-_]?break|interface|breaking|deprecat|remov)\b/. finding.title: tomlStringArray and yamlStringArray are byte-equivalent coercion helpers in two modules
finding.summary: toml.ts's `tomlStringArray` and yaml.ts's `yamlStringArray` have identical bodies — scalar string to `[s]`, array filtered to its string elements, anything else `[]`, then trim and drop empties. Neither is format-specific in any way: both operate on already-parsed JS values, so there is nothing TOML- or YAML-shaped about either. Two names for one function means a behavior question ('do we keep whitespace-only entries?') has to be answered twice and can be answered inconsistently; it also invites a third copy the next time a parser module is added.
evidence: toml.ts:48-56 and yaml.ts:32-40 differ only in the function name; the `typeof value === "string" ? [value] : Array.isArray(value) ? value.filter(...) : []` then `.map(trim).filter(length>0)` body is identical.
Both take `value: unknown` (an already-parsed value), so neither depends on its source format.

finding.title: Required-test rerun discards all test output, so required_test_failed is undiagnosable
finding.summary: rerunRequiredTests spawns each required command with stdio ignore, so stdout/stderr of a failing verification command is destroyed. The only surviving signal is the exit code (or a spawn error message), which then becomes the entire body of the required_test_failed issue surfaced to the host. Confirms obs-remediate-dispatch-001 at HEAD: the finding stands at high/high, unnarrowed.

finding.title: No machine-readable reporter is configured; the only structured run record is an advisory custom reporter
finding.summary: The `test.reporters` array (line 40) is `["default", "./scripts/shared/vitest-timing-reporter.mjs"]`. `default` writes human console prose only, so every structured signal about a run — pass/fail counts, failed file paths, the `runToken` the gate uses to detect a stale ledger — is produced solely by the custom timing reporter's ledger write. finding.title: Two-minute test timeout with no slow-test threshold tuned for it: a hung spawn is indistinguishable from progress
finding.summary: `testTimeout` is 120000ms and `hookTimeout` is 60000ms (lines 44-45), chosen because audit integration tests spawn real CLI subprocesses. finding.title: Potential silent failure when normalizing items
finding.summary: The normalizeItems function (and the broader buildContentCoherenceTrace entry point) throws generic Error objects on validation failures. These are plain Error instances with no structured type/code, so any caller that catches broadly (e.g. catch (e) { /* ignore */ }) can silently drop malformed content-coherence inputs. The mechanism claim is accurate: generic Errors with no distinguishing type make it trivial for upstream handlers to swallow them without diagnostics. Confidence is low because no caller in this file actually swallows the error — the risk is hypothetical and depends on external call sites not visible here.

finding.title: status reports a null elapsed time for an unparseable last-obligation timestamp
finding.summary: cmdStatus guards the per-run durations with Number.isFinite(startMs) && Number.isFinite(endMs) (line 54) but the last-obligation elapsed computation below has no such guard: Date.now() - Date.parse(lastObligationStartedAt) is emitted as last_obligation_elapsed_ms whenever started_at is a non-empty but unparseable string. finding.title: sameLensDedupe and upsertFindingByIdentity collapse findings with no merge trace, unlike crossLensDedupe
finding.summary: crossLensDedupe emits three provenance channels — a mergeMap, an optional `onMerge` callback, and (under global id discipline) a membership-closed dispositionById with the full mergePath — and even enforces evidence conservation at the boundary. The two sibling collapse paths in the same module emit none of it. sameLensDedupe absorbs and filters findings returning only the surviving array, and upsertFindingByIdentity mutates the map entry in place. A finding that disappears from the audit report through either path leaves no record of which finding absorbed it or why, so 'why is this finding not in the report' is unanswerable from artifacts — the exact question a merge log exists to answer. The asymmetry sits inside one file whose stated purpose is a single shared dedup core.

finding.title: rubocop parse failure and per-record drops are silent — a malformed analyzer run is indistinguishable from a clean one
finding.summary: parseRubocop swallows every failure mode without emitting any signal: a JSON.parse throw returns [] from the catch, and each guard clause (non-object file, missing path, non-object offense) drops the record with a bare `continue`. normalizeRubocopJson then hands the empty array to normalizeGenericExternalResults, which produces a well-formed ExternalAnalyzerResults with `results: []` and no tool_statuses. Downstream consumers therefore read 'rubocop ran and found nothing' for a rubocop invocation that in fact failed to parse. The follow-up confirms the original high/high finding STANDS at the reported severity and confidence; the affected scope is precisely the rubocop adapter's parse seam, not the shared normalizer.

finding.title: The friction sink swallows every failure with zero diagnostic, so the observability channel is itself unobservable
finding.summary: UPHELD at HEAD, unchanged in severity/confidence. captureFrictionEvent wraps the whole locked append in a bare `catch {}` whose body is only a comment, and returns Promise<void>, so neither the function nor any caller can observe a lost event. This is the sole mechanical sink (the only in-tree caller is stepBoundaryCapture.ts:189), and the blocking end-of-run triage derives its subject set from that same record (collectTriageSubjects, triage.ts:410-412), so a systematically failing sink degrades into a run that reports zero mechanical friction and closes out green. The best-effort/non-fatal contract for the caller is right and should stand; non-fatal does not require untraceable, and the swallow can still increment an in-process counter or stamp a one-time degraded marker the triage block renders.

finding.title: The fail-closed git-tree message names two possible causes but captures neither the git error nor the exit status
finding.summary: isInsideGitWorkTree discards every diagnostic: the try/catch returns false without inspecting the thrown error, and the success path examines only status and stdout, never stderr or the spawn error field. Both grounding gates then emit a message that says 'git unavailable or not a git work tree' — a disjunction the code already knows the answer to but did not keep. When these gates hard-block promotion (the fail-closed path), the operator is handed a two-branch guess and must re-run git manually to learn which branch fired, e.g. git-not-on-PATH versus a repo_root pointing outside the tree versus a spawn EACCES.

src/remediate/validation/contractPipelineGates.ts:1219 - the blocking message reads 'git unavailable or not a git work tree' — an unresolved disjunction handed to the operator.

finding.title: Tracked-path enumeration degrades to an empty corpus with no observable signal
finding.summary: enumerateTrackedFilePaths returns an empty Set on every git failure mode (git missing, not a repo, non-zero status, spawn throw) and emits no diagnostic, log, or typed failure marker. The empty-corpus state is indistinguishable from a repo that genuinely has no tracked files, yet its downstream effect is total: resolveBasenameToTrackedPath and groundDesignFinding both consult that Set, so every basename citation silently fails to ground. The comment claims the degradation is 'monotonic, never a regression' because callers fall back to existsSync, but that fallback lives in the callers, not here, and nothing records that the corpus was empty for an environmental reason. An operator seeing a run where all design findings came back ungrounded has no artifact-visible way to tell a broken git invocation from genuinely bad citations.

The status check discards `result.stderr` entirely: `if (!result || result.status !== 0 || typeof result.stdout !== "string") {\n    return known;\n  }`
Consumer designFindingGrounding.ts grounds solely on `knownPaths.has(p) || resolveBasenameToTrackedPath(p, knownPaths) !== undefined` — an empty corpus makes both legs false for every citation.

src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:130-132 - a non-zero `result.status` returns the same empty Set as a clean empty repo; `result.stderr` is captured by spawnSync (encoding utf8) but never read or surfaced.

src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:112-114 - the doc comment states the intended contract, 'Degrades to an empty set when git is missing / not a repo', confirming the silence is deliberate and that no signal channel exists.

src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:96-100 - the corpus feeds the M-B3 gate and the remediate basename resolvers, so an unobservable empty corpus propagates into grounding verdicts for every citation.

entries.title: Louvain guard bounds truncate silently, so a non-converged partition is indistinguishable from a converged one
entries.rationale: Finding excluded by the intent checkpoint (filter or excluded scope).

finding.title: Louvain guard bounds truncate silently, so a non-converged partition is indistinguishable from a converged one
finding.summary: Both loops in the clustering backbone carry anti-runaway guards that exit by falling out of the while condition and returning the partial result as if it were the fixed point: localMoving stops after `graph.nodes.length + 8` passes and louvain stops after `base.nodes.length + 4` levels. Neither records that the bound was hit, and Partition (a bare Map) has nowhere to carry that fact. The consumer is scale-stability scoring across the resolution sweep — a truncated partition at one rung silently distorts the 'this boundary persists across resolutions' conclusion that the whole design-review overlay rests on. The module is explicitly pure/no-IO so logging is out of scope, but the guard hit is a returnable value, not a log line. The early `if (nextGraph.nodes.length === current.nodes.length) break;` aggregation exit is the same class.
evidence: src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:212-215 — `let guard = 0; const maxPasses = graph.nodes.length + 8; while (improved && guard < maxPasses) {` — exiting on the guard is indistinguishable from exiting on `!improved`.
src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:372-374 — `let guard = 0; const maxLevels = base.nodes.length + 4; while (guard < maxLevels) {` with no post-loop check of `guard === maxLevels`.
src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:364 — `export function louvain(graph: WeightedGraph, resolution: number): Partition` — the return type cannot carry a convergence flag.
src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:408 — resolutionSweep returns Partition[] only, so a truncated rung is invisible to the stability scorer.
runtime:unit:src-shared: not_confirmed — Deterministic runtime command failed with exit code 1: npm test
reproduction: Construct a weight pattern that keeps localMoving improving past nodes.length + 8 passes: the returned Partition is byte-shaped like a converged one and resolutionSweep reports nothing unusual.

finding.title: The file-integrity io_errors bucket records only a path — the failure code and the missing/io_error discriminator are lost before reporting
finding.summary: checkAffectedFileIntegrity (src/remediate/utils/fileIntegrity.ts:162-205) classifies a path as io_error purely from a falsy return: `const currentHash = await hashAffectedPath(root, record.path); if (!currentHash) return { kind: "io_error" };` (lines 187-188). hashAffectedPath already caught and swallowed the underlying error itself (lines 138-146, and inside hashFile at lines 51-54), so the outer catch's ENOENT branch at line 192 is effectively unreachable for read failures raised inside it: a file deleted between the existsSync probe (line 137) and the read is reported as io_error, never as missing. Worse, a path that stats as neither a file nor a directory (socket, fifo, dangling special) returns undefined from lines 140-142 with NO reportHashIoError call at all, so it lands in io_errors with zero diagnostic anywhere. The consumer surface then prints only the bare path — src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2487 renders `io-error: ${p}` — leaving an operator with a path, no errno, and no way to tell a permissions problem from a race or an unusual file type.

finding.title: Runtime-validation evidence is truncated to the LAST 10 output lines, discarding the diagnostic head of a failure
finding.summary: runCommand captures the full stdout+stderr of the deterministic runtime command but persists only the last 10 lines as `evidence` (lines 59-64 on the error path and 76-81 on the close path). finding.title: StateStore validates state.json on read but never on write, so an invalid state persists and bricks the next load

StateStore (src/remediate/state/store.ts:246-261) supplies only `parse`; no `validate` is passed. Every write path (`mutate` line 295, `saveState` line 312) therefore persists whatever the caller produced without running `validateState`. The same `validateState` rules are enforced on the way back in (parse, lines 252-259) and THROW.
